lines.text: Part two: how does AI actually use embeddings?
Quick recap: an embedding model turns a word's meaning into a list of numbers.
That whole list is the embedding.
Squash all those numbers down to two, and each word gets a spot on a map.
Similar meanings land close together.
Dog and puppy are neighbours. Pizza? Way over here.
A computer can score how close two spots are.
Dog and puppy: point eight. Dog and pizza: point three five.
Pizza isn't zero, because scores are fuzzy. What matters is which is closest.
That score has a name: cosine similarity.
Picture each embedding as an arrow. It measures the angle between two arrows.
Dog and puppy: a small angle, so a high score.
Dog and pizza: a wider angle, so a lower score.
Pointing the same way scores one. At a right angle, zero.
So why use them? Search.
Keyword search spots the word bike, and gets it wrong.
Embedding search matches the meaning, and finds the fix.
Where do embeddings live? In a database.
Take a team handbook and split it into chunks.
Each row stores a chunk and its numbers.
A vector database searches those numbers by closeness.
Ask a question, and it becomes numbers too.
The database finds the nearest chunk.
That chunk goes to Claude, along with your question.
So Claude answers from the right page.
So that's embeddings: meaning, turned into numbers.
